what_its_for: Oxycodone is a strong prescription pain medicine (opioid) used to treat moderate to severe pain that other pain medicines have not controlled well enough. It may be used for pain from surgery, injury, or ongoing conditions like cancer.
how_to_take: Take oxycodone exactly as your doctor prescribes. Swallow tablets or capsules whole — do not crush, chew, break, or dissolve them, especially extended-release forms, as this can release a dangerous amount of medicine all at once. You can take it with or without food, but if it upsets your stomach, try taking it with food or milk. Never share your medicine with anyone else. Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest time possible.
dosing: Your dose is set by your doctor based on your pain level, your medical history, and how your body responds to the medicine. Do not change your dose on your own. Immediate-release oxycodone is usually taken every 4 to 6 hours as needed. Extended-release (long-acting) oxycodone is taken every 12 hours on a regular schedule. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions.
missed_dose: If you are taking oxycodone on a regular schedule and miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — UNLESS it is almost time for your next dose. If that is the case, skip the missed dose and go back to your regular schedule. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are taking it only as needed for pain, take it when you need it and follow your doctor's instructions.
storage: Store oxycodone at room temperature, away from heat, moisture, and light. Keep it in a secure location — ideally a locked medicine cabinet — out of reach of children, teenagers, and anyone who was not prescribed this medicine. Do not store it in the bathroom. When you no longer need the medicine, dispose of it safely. You can use a medication take-back program or a drug disposal kiosk at many pharmacies. If none is available, mix unused pills with an undesirable substance like dirt or coffee grounds in a sealed bag and throw them in the trash.
what_to_avoid: Do not drink alcohol while taking oxycodone — combining them can slow your breathing and may be life-threatening. Avoid other medicines that make you drowsy, such as sleeping pills, anti-anxiety medicines, muscle relaxers, and other pain medicines, unless your doctor approves them. Do not drive, operate heavy machinery, or do anything that requires you to be alert until you know how this medicine affects you. Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice, as it may increase the amount of oxycodone in your blood. Do not stop taking oxycodone suddenly without talking to your doctor, as this can cause withdrawal symptoms.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or get emergency help right away if you or someone around you experiences: slow, shallow, or stopped breathing; extreme sleepiness or difficulty waking up; blue or purplish color on the lips or fingertips; severe dizziness or fainting; chest pain; seizures; or signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, swelling of the face or throat, or difficulty breathing. Also call your doctor if you develop severe constipation, confusion, mood changes, or if your pain is not controlled. If you suspect an overdose, call 911 immediately and use naloxone (Narcan) if it is available.
when_it_works: Immediate-release oxycodone usually starts to relieve pain within 15 to 30 minutes after you take it, and it works for about 4 to 6 hours. Extended-release oxycodone takes longer to start working but provides pain relief over a 12-hour period. Do not expect the medicine to work faster by taking more — this is dangerous.
special_populations: Older adults (65 and over): You may be more sensitive to oxycodone's effects, especially dizziness and breathing problems. Your doctor may start you on a lower dose. Children: Oxycodone is generally only prescribed to children in specific situations under close medical supervision. Pregnancy: Oxycodone can harm an unborn baby and may cause life-threatening withdrawal symptoms in a newborn. Tell your doctor right away if you are pregnant or plan to become pregnant. Breastfeeding: Oxycodone passes into breast milk and can harm a nursing baby. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding. Kidney or liver problems: Your doctor may need to adjust your dose or monitor you more closely if you have kidney or liver disease.
